title: Async queries and the request's CancellationToken
summary: ToListAsync, FirstOrDefaultAsync and SaveChangesAsync with the token ASP.NET Core gives every request, and one context doing one thing at a time.

steps.title: Async all the way, with the request's token
body: Earlier lessons used `ToList()` and `SaveChanges()` to keep the focus on EF itself. In a web API that is the wrong default. A synchronous query **blocks a thread-pool thread** while the database works; under load the pool runs dry, requests queue, and latency climbs although the CPU is idle. The async methods give the thread back while waiting:
```csharp fragment
app.MapGet("/orders/{id:int}", async (int id, ShopDb db, CancellationToken ct) =>
await db.Orders.AsNoTracking().FirstOrDefaultAsync(o => o.Id == id, ct) is { } order
? Results.Ok(order)
: Results.NotFound());
app.MapPost("/orders", async (Order order, ShopDb db, CancellationToken ct) =>
db.Orders.Add(order);
await db.SaveChangesAsync(ct);
return Results.Created($"/orders/{order.Id}", order);

The `CancellationToken` parameter is filled in by ASP.NET Core with `HttpContext.RequestAborted`: it fires when the client disconnects (closed tab, mobile app gave up, load balancer timeout). Pass it to **every** async EF call (`ToListAsync(ct)`, `CountAsync(ct)`, `SingleOrDefaultAsync(..., ct)`, `SaveChangesAsync(ct)`), and EF cancels the command on the database, so a report nobody is waiting for stops using a connection and CPU. In MVC controllers, add a `CancellationToken` parameter to the action the same way.

Cancellation surfaces as an `OperationCanceledException` (or its subclass `TaskCanceledException`). ASP.NET Core does not log it as an unhandled error when the request was aborted; do not catch and swallow it in your own code.

steps.prompt: A user starts a 20-second export, then closes the tab after 2 seconds. The endpoint awaits `db.Orders.Where(...).ToListAsync(ct)` with the request's token. What happens?
options: The token fires, EF cancels the running command, and the endpoint stops with an OperationCanceledException that nobody sees
The query runs to the end; the result is thrown away when the response cannot be sent
The database rolls back every transaction of that user
ASP.NET Core kills the thread running the query
steps.explain: That is the point of passing `ct`. Without it, the database keeps working for 18 more seconds for nobody, holding a pooled connection the whole time.

steps.prompt: Complete the endpoint so the query is async and stops when the client goes away.
steps.code: app.MapGet("/orders", async (ShopDb db, CancellationToken ct) => await db.Orders.AsNoTracking().OrderBy(o => o.Id).__1__(__2__));
steps.explain: `CancellationToken.None` compiles but throws the request's token away; `ToList()` would block a thread.

steps.prompt: The token is already cancelled when the query starts (the client left while the request waited for a connection). What does this print?
code: protected override void OnConfiguring(DbContextOptionsBuilder options) => options.UseSqlite("Data Source=shop.db");
steps.explain: EF checks the token before it sends anything, so no command reaches the database. A token that fires mid-query cancels the command instead.

steps.title: One context, one operation at a time
body: A `DbContext` is not thread-safe, and it runs **one** database operation at a time. This looks like a clever speed-up and is a bug:
```csharp fragment
// Two queries "in parallel" on the same context
var customers = db.Customers.CountAsync(ct);
var orders = db.Orders.CountAsync(ct);
await Task.WhenAll(customers, orders);
On SQL Server or PostgreSQL the second call fails with:
```text
System.InvalidOperationException: A second operation was started on this context instance before a
previous operation completed. This is usually caused by different threads concurrently using the same
instance of DbContext.

Await each call before starting the next. If you really need parallel queries, use a separate context for each (inject `IDbContextFactory<ShopDb>` and `CreateDbContext()` per task). The same rule bites in background work: a `BackgroundService` or a `Task.Run` must create its own scope or context, never reuse the request's.
Also never block on async code with `.Result` or `.Wait()`: it ties up a thread exactly like the sync call did, and can deadlock in code with a synchronization context.

steps.title: Count them one after the other
prompt: The dashboard's `Counts` method uses `Task.WhenAll` on one context. SQLite's driver happens to finish its async calls synchronously, so it does not crash **here**, but against the production SQL Server it throws the *second operation* exception from the card.
Rewrite `Counts` to await the two counts **one after the other**, passing `ct` to both. It returns `(customers, orders)`.
solution: static async Task<(int Customers, int Orders)> Counts(ShopDb db, CancellationToken ct)
template: dojoDb.Orders.AddRange(new Order { Customer = dojoAna, TotalCents = 4500 }, new Order { Customer = dojoAna, TotalCents = 900 }, new Order { Customer = dojoAna, TotalCents = 1200 });
protected override void OnConfiguring(DbContextOptionsBuilder options) => options.UseSqlite("Data Source=shop.db");

require.message: Awaits the customer count with ct
Awaits the order count with ct

hints: Then the same for orders, and return the tuple.
steps.explain: Two round trips one after the other cost a millisecond or two more than the parallel version would. If that matters, the fix is one query that returns both counts, not two contexts.

steps.prompt: This appears in the logs of a `BackgroundService` that sends reminder emails. What is wrong?
code: System.ObjectDisposedException: Cannot access a disposed context instance. A common cause of this error is
disposing a context instance that was resolved from dependency injection and then later trying to use the
same context instance elsewhere in your application.
options: The worker kept a context from a scope that has ended; it should create its own scope (or use IDbContextFactory) for each run
SaveChangesAsync was called without a CancellationToken
steps.explain: A `BackgroundService` is a singleton; `ShopDb` is scoped. Resolve it inside the loop with `using var scope = scopes.CreateScope();` (inject `IServiceScopeFactory`) or call `factory.CreateDbContext()`, and dispose it after each batch.

steps.title: An orders API, async end to end
prompt: Build the orders API with async EF calls that all take the request's token. **Run checks** starts your server and calls it.
- Register `ShopDb` with `AddDbContext` and `Data Source=orders.db`; create the database at start-up in a scope (fine for this exercise; production uses migrations, lesson 4).
- `GET /orders`: all orders by id, **no tracking**, with `ToListAsync(ct)`.
Every handler takes `CancellationToken ct`. No `ToList()`, `SaveChanges()`, `.Result` or `.Wait()`.

await db.Orders.AsNoTracking().FirstOrDefaultAsync(o => o.Id == id, ct) is { } order
app.MapPost("/orders", async (Order order, ShopDb db, CancellationToken ct) =>

var dojoA = await http.PostAsJsonAsync("/orders", new { customer = "ana@mail.test", totalCents = 4500 });
Dojo.Eq("the first order gets id 1", "1", DojoWeb.Prop(await DojoWeb.Json(dojoA), "id"));
dojoList.ValueKind == JsonValueKind.Array ? string.Join("|", dojoList.EnumerateArray().Select(o => DojoWeb.Prop(o, "customer"))) : "(not an array)");

`await db.Orders.AsNoTracking().FirstOrDefaultAsync(o => o.Id == id, ct) is { } order ? Results.Ok(order) : Results.NotFound()`
steps.explain: This is the shape of every EF Core endpoint you will write at work: async, token passed through, no tracking for reads.
